problem: Prior generalist robot policies (RT-X/Octo for manipulation, GNM/ViNT/NoMaD for navigation) are each trained on one family of similar embodiments. It is unknown whether very different embodiments, such as wheeled/legged/aerial navigators and robot arms, can be pooled into one policy with positive transfer, given their different hardware, viewpoints and action spaces.
motivation: Pooling heterogeneous robot data would let data from one domain help another without recollection, which is especially relevant for mobile manipulators. The driving observation concerns egocentric cameras (a wrist camera on an arm, a forward camera on a navigator). With such cameras, both domains have the same equivariance between camera-pose changes and image changes (moving 'left' transforms the image the same way). Both also rely on visual servoing and collision/geometry reasoning, so both can be framed as goal-image reaching.
key_idea: Cast manipulation and navigation as a single image-goal-reaching problem in a shared, roughly camera-aligned 7-D action frame. Then co-train one diffusion-policy transformer on a 50/50 mix of OXE manipulation data and GNM/driving navigation data, and measure transfer in both directions.
insight: Navigation data helps goal-conditioned manipulation mostly on spatial-reasoning / OOD tasks. Co-training vs Manip-only: Novel Cluttered Grasp 50% vs 20%, Shelf 65% vs 30%. The benefit depends on goal conditioning: the goal-conditioned gap is 55% vs 20%, while without goal conditioning it is 45% vs 40%. Linear probes (CCA R^2) show co-trained features correlate more strongly with temporal distance-to-goal (0.740 vs 0.703 on Novel Cluttered). This suggests navigation data regularizes representations toward current-to-goal spatial relations. In the per-dataset GNM ablation, indoor/sidewalk navigation data transfers to manipulation far better than trail/off-road data: SACSoN gives 70% Cluttered Grasp, while Tartan and Seattle give 10% and 5%. Other findings: third-person co-training is important for wrist-camera policies (Toy Kitchen 80% vs 25%); larger models help (27M→186M); RT-1-style 256-bin discretization essentially fails below ~180M params. The reverse direction (manipulation→navigation) gives only a small, noisy gain of 5-7%, which the authors admit may be within run-to-run variance.
method: Unified goal-reaching formulation: every task is π(a_{t:t+k-1} | o_{t-c+1:t}, o_g). Goal images are sampled uniformly 20–40 timesteps ahead in the same trajectory, so ideally the action approximates the camera-pose delta toward the goal.

Action-frame alignment: each dataset's actions are normalized to [-1,1]. Manipulation actions are 7-D (delta xyz, delta rotation, gripper), with dimensions/signs manually swapped per OXE dataset after visually inspecting (obs, action, next obs) triples. Navigation actions are 5 future egocentric (x,y) waypoints mapped into the manipulation frame as (0, a[1], -a[0], 0,0,0,0): nav forward → manip downward (-z, wrist camera looks down), nav left → manip left.

Data mixture: 9 OXE manipulation datasets (Bridge, Fractal, Taco Play, Jaco Play, Roboturk, NYU Door, Viola, Berkeley UR5, Toto) plus an own WidowX/ViperX VR-teleop dataset (text says 400 trajectories over 8 h; appendix says 300). Navigation comes from GNM datasets (GO Stanford, SCAND, RECON, Cory Hall, Seattle, TartanDrive), SACSoN and subsampled BDD100k. Sampling is upweighted to ~50% navigation / 50% manipulation, and third-person and wrist views are randomly mixed for OXE.

Architecture (NoMaD-style): one EfficientNet-b5 encodes the observation history; a second EfficientNet-b5 encodes the current+goal image stacked channel-wise. Tokens pass through a Transformer (8 layers, 8 heads, hidden 2048). A 1D U-Net diffusion head (10 denoising iterations) outputs an action chunk (b, n, 7), and an MLP head predicts temporal distance to goal. The main model has ~186M params.
Loss: diffusion denoising loss + λ·MSE temporal-distance loss with λ=0.001. Trained ~48 GPU-hours on one 48 GB GPU (batch 256, lr 1e-4, cosine schedule).

Navigation deployment: a topological map of images is recorded at 4 Hz by driving the robot through the environment beforehand. The distance head localizes the robot to the closest node and picks a subgoal slightly ahead. Predicted waypoints are converted into linear/angular velocity commands.

Mobile manipulator (Mobile ALOHA, zero-shot embodiment): the same policy runs twice, once on the base camera for navigation and once on the right-arm wrist camera for manipulation. Control is handed to the arm when the robot is near the final goal and predicted actions become small.

setting.backbone: EfficientNet-b5 image encoders + Transformer + diffusion-policy (U-Net) action head + MLP distance head, trained on cross-embodiment robot data (NoMaD-style architecture)
setting.training_data: Real robot demonstrations only. Manipulation: 9 Open X-Embodiment datasets plus an own WidowX250s/ViperX300s VR-teleop dataset (400 trajectories / 8 h in main text; 300 in appendix; ~1.3% of the mix). Navigation/driving: GNM datasets (GO Stanford, SCAND, RECON, Cory Hall, Seattle, TartanDrive), SACSoN and subsampled BDD100k. Sampled ~50% navigation / 50% manipulation (GNM 46.3%, BDD100k 10%).
setting.observation: monocular egocentric RGB history + goal image (forward-facing camera for navigation, wrist camera for manipulation; third-person OXE views mixed in during training)
setting.action_space: unified 7-D continuous action chunk. Navigation: 5 future egocentric (x,y) waypoints, converted to linear/angular velocities. Manipulation: delta end-effector position/rotation + gripper.
setting.privileged: Pre-exploration: a prior topological map of goal images recorded at 4 Hz by moving the robot through the test environment, with coverage ensured. No GPS/pose/semantic maps. Manipulation goal images are collected by teleoperating to the goal state.

numbers_note: No standard embodied-navigation benchmarks are used; all results are small-scale custom real-world evaluations. The main body shows results only in figures; exact numbers come from appendix tables. Several inconsistencies exist between text and tables. (1) The text claims ~80% average navigation success over 4 embodiments and 95% for DJI Tello (GNM + Driving + Manip and GNM-only), but the appendix table gives Tello 40/40% and 65/80%. (2) Clearpath Jackal results are described only as relative differences ('12%, 7% and 1% better'), with no absolute numbers in any table. (3) Captions state 19%/13% improvements vs 20%/5-7% in the text. (4) The navigation table also has a 'GNM + M3ED + BDD + Manip' row (LoCoBot 85/97%, Tello 40/57%, Go1 53/35%), but the M3ED dataset is never described. (5) The own dataset size is 400 trajectories in the text vs 300 in the appendix. Scaling tables (27M–186M params) are given for manipulation and navigation; the 186M row equals the main GNM + Driving + Manip row. The 112M model is better on navigation (LoCoBot 90/85, Tello 65/50, Go1 58/73). The last column header in the manipulation scaling table is duplicated ('Cluttered Grasp', presumably Shelf). Ablation tables for goal conditioning, third-person co-training, discretization and per-GNM-dataset co-training are also reported. The 'Coll.' metric unit is not defined (likely average collisions per run).
results: A single 186M-param goal-conditioned diffusion policy controls a WidowX arm, LoCoBot, Jackal, Go1 quadruped, DJI Tello drone (unseen) and Mobile ALOHA (unseen, 50% on Egg Nav/Pick/Place). It averages 71% over 5 manipulation tasks. Adding navigation+driving data improves manipulation by ~20% absolute over the Manip-only ablation, with the biggest gains on Novel Cluttered Grasp (50 vs 20%) and Shelf (65 vs 30%). Adding manipulation data to navigation yields only a claimed 5-7% average gain over GNM-only, with mixed per-robot table numbers (e.g. Tello GNM-only is better). No external baselines are compared; all comparisons are own data-mixture ablations.
limitations: Actions are a coarse shared end-effector/waypoint abstraction with manually aligned axes. It cannot handle robots needing varying degrees of freedom (e.g., multi-fingered hands), and a quadruped is controlled only by heading.

Only image-goal conditioning with a pre-recorded topological map for navigation (no language goals). Evaluations are small real-world trials with high variance, and the authors admit the 5-7% navigation gain may be noise.
A small in-domain manipulation dataset is still required for the target arm. Text/table inconsistencies (Tello 95% vs 40%, missing Jackal numbers) weaken the navigation claims.
